title: How to Turn Your Marketing Internship into a Full-Time Job - University of New Hampshire
content: Paige Spencer ’26, center, with Office Interiors Limited President Ellen Bates, left, and Director of Design Erin King at the company’s Dover, New Hampshire, office. Heading into her final semester, marketing student Paige Spencer '26 was looking for an internship where she could gain real-world experience while completing her senior capstone project, which challenges students to help a business improve its marketing efforts. At the same time, Ellen Bates, president of Dover-based Office Interiors Limited, attended a UNH CEO & Family Enterprise Center meeting where Cayce Jones, director of UNH Paul College Career and Professional Success, spoke about the value interns can bring to small businesses. Bates decided it was time to act. Her women-led commercial interior design and furniture firm needed someone who could "change its marketing game." Office Interiors then posted the internship on employment website Handshake seeking its own version of Emily in Paris—the Netflix series about a young marketing professional documenting her experiences on social media. What followed was a perfect match. Spencer turned the internship into a full-time marketing coordinator position while helping the 40-year-old company modernize its digital presence. Rather than applying through the posting, Spencer reached out directly to Bates with her qualifications and a creative video introducing herself. "She showed initiative by figuring out who I was and emailing me directly. On top of that, she created a video of herself from locations around the world, including the Eiffel Tower. We had specifically encouraged applicants to stand out in the posting — to be creative and show us who they were — and Paige did that in full force,” Bates says. Spencer didn't want to be just another applicant. Instead, she focused on getting in front of the people making the hiring decision. “As soon as I saw the opportunity, I thought, 'This seems like a great company, I need to meet them,'" Spencer says. Office Interiors had an inconsistent social media presence and a website that didn't fully showcase its work. Spencer tackled both. “When I started, there was an opportunity to modernize the company’s digital presence and better showcase its work,” Spencer says. “We refreshed social media, focused on growing our audience, and from there, my role expanded into broader marketing and brand strategy.” One of Spencer's proudest achievements was rebuilding the company's website from scratch—even though she had never designed one before. She taught herself the process through online tutorials and experimentation, then focused on creating a more visual website that used photos and video to better showcase Office Interiors' work. "The website was a big win. We're always busy doing great work, and we have so much talent and so many projects to showcase,” says Erin King, director of design at Office Interiors. “Paige took that content and turned it into something worthy of a website. We worked together to gather the photos, and she pulled it all together. I think it's one of our best tools because people don't cold call anymore. The website is our face — it's our cold call." Bates and King say Spencer struck a balance between collaboration and initiative. She wasn't afraid to ask questions, but she was equally comfortable taking ownership of new projects. "It became obvious during her internship that when she graduated, we had to keep her. There was no question about it," Bates says. Building the company's new website was only the beginning. In her full-time role, Spencer continued expanding Office Interiors' marketing efforts by developing a social media strategy centered on three content pillars: educating customers about the design process, showcasing completed projects,  and giving followers a behind-the-scenes look at the company's culture. Her role also grew beyond digital marketing. She began tracking marketing analytics, representing Office Interiors at networking events, and helping plan company initiatives, including its upcoming 40th anniversary celebration and fundraiser. "I liked social media and content marketing. Now that I'm doing it, I kind of love all parts of marketing," Spencer says. "We wear a lot of different hats. But I love it. No day is the same." Bates says Spencer's willingness to keep learning has benefited both her career and the company. The new website and her broader marketing efforts have already generated new business and helped raise Office Interiors' profile. "Paige is becoming the face of Office Interiors when it comes to marketing," Bates says. "She's representing us at networking events and with the organizations we're involved in, in addition to everything she does in the office. We're asking a lot of her." Looking back, Spencer says her biggest piece of advice is to treat the internship search like the first step in your career “Research the company first and make sure it’s a place where you can see yourself growing,” Spencer says. “Then go all in. Find ways to stand out, take initiative, and look for problems you can help solve. Don’t just treat an internship like something to put on your résumé, treat it like the first step in your career.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

content: eHealth, Inc. EHTH recently said small and mid-sized employers are facing a sharp jump in health insurance costs for 2027, pushing many to rethink traditional group coverage. Its survey of more than 500 business owners and managers found that 54% expect premium increases of at least 10%, while more than one in five face hikes of 15% or higher. Last month, Aon plc AON projected that U.S. employer healthcare costs will rise 9.5% in 2027 before employers take steps to rein in expenses. Aon links the increase not only to higher prices but also to greater healthcare utilization and a more expensive mix of services. Marsh & McLennan Companies, Inc. MRSH expects an even steeper 11% increase before cost-control measures, moderating to 8.2% after employers make planned benefit changes. That would mark the sharpest increase in employer health benefit costs since 2003, even after cost-containment efforts. Marsh also found that 59% of employers plan benefit changes, including higher deductibles, as companies try to contain spending. It attributes the expected increase to several factors, including costly new therapies, higher provider rates, broader use of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, AI-supported medical billing and out-of-network charges. GLP-1 drugs alone are projected to contribute roughly one percentage point to health benefit cost growth in 2027. eHealth CEO Derrick Duke said that rising costs are making it harder for employers to use health benefits to attract and retain workers. The company sees growing interest in alternatives such as Custom Health Option and Individual Care Expense (CHOICE) Arrangements, also known as Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangements (ICHRAs), which can offer employers more cost certainty, flexibility and simpler administration. The numbers suggest that higher premiums are starting to change how smaller employers think about providing health benefits. Among companies facing rate increases, 80% said the size of the hike surprised them. The bigger concern is that 73% are considering moving away from traditional group coverage in 2027. Another 85% worry they may be unable to afford group coverage within three years. Meanwhile, 58% are already pursuing alternatives, while awareness of CHOICE Arrangements rose to 57% from 46% a year earlier, a meaningful eleven-point increase. For eHealth, this trend could expand the market for employer-funded individual coverage. If more small and mid-sized companies move away from fully insured group plans, demand could rise for CHOICE Arrangements and other options that eHealth can help employers and workers evaluate. That could expand lead volumes, policy enrollments and commission opportunities. The survey also suggests that employers have reasons beyond premiums to consider alternatives: 79% view plan administration as a burden, while 72% report at least one dissatisfaction with current coverage. eHealth currently has a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). Centene says ICHRA adoption among businesses rose 34% from 2024 to 2025, signaling stronger interest in the model. Through Ambetter Health Solutions, CNC is targeting this opportunity with ICHRA-compatible plans available in 13 states in 2026. Continued adoption could help Centene attract additional members, lift premium revenues and broaden its reach in the employer-linked individual market. Last fall, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill School of Law reportedly used ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok as jurors in a mock trial based on a real juvenile case. At the same time, AI-powered jury research platforms are entering the litigation consulting market, offering attorneys and claims professionals rapid assessments of liability, comparative fault, and potential damages. These tools can provide valuable early insights. They may help legal teams test competing narratives, identify themes that resonate and flag arguments that could be poorly received, all faster and at a lower cost than traditional jury research. However, lawyers should distinguish reliability from validity. An AI simulation may consistently measure individual reactions to a case summary yet still fail to capture how an actual jury reaches a verdict. Real jurors discuss evidence, challenge each other’s assumptions, and revise their views through deliberation. Venue-specific attitudes and community norms also shape outcomes in ways that broad simulated populations may not reflect. AI jury research is therefore best viewed as a screening tool rather than a substitute for focus groups, mock trials, or other interactive methods. It can inform early case assessment and help counsel decide where deeper research is warranted, but its polished percentages and damages ranges should not be mistaken for predictions of an actual verdict. For legal teams, the key question is not whether AI or traditional research is categorically better, it is whether the chosen method measures the issue that matters. When a case turns on contested evidence, group dynamics, and collective judgment, human deliberation remains central. title: UNH increases financial aid, awarding record $40 million to incoming class - Concord Monitor
content:
The Concord Monitor is a Pulitzer Prize winning daily newspaper and website located in the capital city of New Hampshire. The Concord Monitor is Central NH's dominant media with more than 70 percent household penetration. The Monitor is a key source of news and information for Concord, NH. The incoming class attending the University of New Hampshire was awarded $40 million in financial aid, the most given in the university’s history. Last year, 88% of the freshman class received financial aid, with an average award of $12,400. This year, that average climbed to more than $16,000, with almost every enrolled student — 96% — receiving aid, according to university spokesperson Tania deLuzuriaga. The increase in aid was not due to more public funding, said Kimberly DeRego, vice provost of enrollment management. Rather, DeRego said, the university made changes to its guidelines around financial aid that allowed it to increase some of its merit and need-based scholarships. Additionally, more students who applied and decided to attend UNH this year were eligible for these scholarships: The class of 2030 had an average high school GPA of 3.7 and enrolled 322 students in UNH’s Hamel Honors and Scholars College, a 20% increase over last year, according to the university. DeRego said more students demonstrated greater need as well. Award-winning coverage on breaking news and today’s top stories in and around the Capital Region. From Arts and Life to Sports and Opinion you’ll have unlimited access to the Concord Monitor's content. Families have expressed concerns about affordability for years, DeRego said. Improving financial aid has been an ongoing effort for the university. “We lose a lot of students to out-of-state institutions because they’re able to give more financial aid,” deLuzuriaga said. “When you take cost out of the equation, they can pick the program that they feel like is really truly best for them.” Last year, in-state tuition at UNH was $19,202, according to the U.S. Department of Education’s College Navigator. Out-of-state tuition was $39,852. “We’re hoping that for our families, it helps them to realize college is attainable for more students,” DeRego said. “I think that’s our hope, and that’s why we do these policies.” Yasmeen is the education reporter at the Concord Monitor. title: UNH Vs. HUM: Which Insurer Stock Has More Upside After CMS Reverses Wall Street’s Biggest Medicare Rate Fear? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth, Inc. (UNH) and Humana, Inc. (HUM) are back in the spotlight on Tuesday after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) lifted Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, with Wall Street estimates pointing to a clear frontrunner. UNH stock rose 8% in extended trading, while HUM stock gained 11%. Over the past year, however, UNH has fallen about 45% and HUM nearly 27%, with both stocks underperforming the broader Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLV), which climbed 10% over the same period. The CMS finalized a 2.48% increase in Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, up from the January proposal that kept rates roughly flat and wiped out nearly $100 billion in market value across major insurers. The updated policy is expected to add more than $13 billion in additional funding to Medicare Advantage plans next year, the CMS said. With the policy overhang removed, attention has shifted back to valuation targets, which point to higher implied upside for UnitedHealth than for Humana. Based on Koyfin estimates, UnitedHealth carries a 12-month average price target of $357.81, implying a 27% upside from the stock’s last close. Coverage across 29 analysts includes 7 ‘Strong Buy’, 16 ‘Buy’, 4 ‘Hold’ and 2 ‘Sell’ ratings. Earlier this month, Raymond James upgraded the stock to ‘Outperform’ with a $330 price target, citing potential upside from expense trends and expected margin improvement at Optum Health, the company’s care delivery arm. Meanwhile, Bernstein SocGen Group reiterated an ‘Outperform’ rating with a $405 target, pointing to UnitedHealth’s expanding AI strategy. The company recently launched its generative AI companion, Avery, as part of broader efforts to reduce operating costs across its insurance segment, where it plans nearly $1 billion in expense cuts and is closing or divesting about 550 Optum Health clinics. UnitedHealth also expects to lose as many as 2.8 million insurance members this year, with revenue potentially declining for the first time since the 1980s as longtime chair and former CEO Stephen Hemsley leads a turnaround effort. The stock still remains below the level at which Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway built its stake last year and faces scrutiny over Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment practices following a Senate committee review. Humana’s upside appears more modest based on Koyfin estimates, with a 12-month average price target of $212.17, implying a 16% upside from current levels. Among 27 covering analysts, the stock carries 2 ‘Strong Buy’, 6 ‘Buy’, 17 ‘Hold’ and 2 ‘Sell’ ratings. Earlier this year, the company projected adjusted 2026 earnings of at least $9 per share, below consensus expectations of $11.87, while the insurer said margins in its individual Medicare Advantage business could remain just below break-even this year. Several brokerages subsequently lowered price targets, with UBS and BofA maintaining ‘Neutral’ ratings after Humana’s 2026 EPS outlook came in roughly 24% below consensus. On the other hand, Morgan Stanley warned that uncertainty around the size of Humana’s 2026 membership cohort remains a risk “particularly heading into 2027 and beyond.” Cantor Fitzgerald said the stock may remain range-bound until clearer membership data emerges in the second quarter, and Guggenheim said it was taking “a prudent view” of the company’s 2027 earnings outlook. Still, Humana expects enrollment in its individual Medicare Advantage plans to increase about 25% in 2026 compared with last year, with over 70% of new members coming from competing plans. One of the safest blue chips to double In a couple years.” Another user noted that “this $13B increase provides critical revenue relief, offsetting rising medical costs and securing sector stability.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Last week, Marvell shares rose 13%, Kosmos Energy edged up about 0.3%, and Hologic ended marginally lower. Hologic shares gained as investors positioned ahead of the company’s planned April 7 takeover by investment firms Blackstone and TPG, after the company said it had received all required regulatory approvals. As of 10.15 p.m. ET, Nasdaq 100 futures were down 0.8%, while S&P 500 futures were down by 0.6%. Dow futures were down 0.4%. Speaking at a White House conference on Monday, Trump reiterated that the U.S. military could target Iranian bridges and power plants if the strait is not reopened by 8 p.m. ET Tuesday. He said negotiations were “going well,” but added that restoring access through Hormuz remains a “very big priority.” He also said that while he would like the U.S. to “take the oil,” Americans ultimately want U.S. forces to return home. The U.S., Iran and regional mediators are reportedly exploring a possible 45-day ceasefire that could open the door to a settlement, while Washington and Tehran are also supposedly reviewing a Pakistan-brokered proposal to restore navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. However, Tehran has said it would only accept ceasefire terms that include a permanent end to the war, sanctions relief, reconstruction commitments and guarantees around safe navigation through the strait. It also warned that strikes on civilian infrastructure could trigger retaliatory attacks on energy facilities across the Gulf. TSLA stock fell more than 2% on Monday, marking its lowest level in nearly seven months. GLJ Research analyst Gordon Johnson said on X that Tesla has broken below its 20, 50 and 75-day moving averages and remains trapped in a descending channel that began after the stock’s December highs near $480. He added that Fibonacci levels point to $322 as the next key support, while momentum indicators indicate the stock is not yet oversold. He also noted that Tesla’s car sales declined year-over-year in both 2024 and 2025 and are expected to fall again in 2026. “$TSLA has made literally NO PROGRESS on ‘robotaxis’ since launching in Austin in June of last yr. It could fall another 70-80%, and STILL be massively overvalued,” Johnson said, adding that the stock trades as 288x estimated 2026 earnings versus 31x for the Magnificent Seven. Johnson’s technical warning follows a bearish update from JPMorgan analyst Ryan Brinkman, who reiterated an ‘Underweight’ rating and set a $145 price target after Tesla’s Q1 delivery report, implying a 60% downside to current levels. “We ... advise investors approach TSLA shares with a high degree of caution,” Brinkman said. He also lowered 2026 earnings per share (EPS) estimate to $1.8 from $2, below consensus expectations, citing risks to demand, execution and competition as Tesla expands into lower-priced, higher-volume vehicle segments. Future Fund Managing Partner Gary Black said on X, “TSLA bulls out in full force today attacking Ryan Brinkman the person. Tesla also deployed 8.8 gigawatt-hours of energy-storage products, down from 10.4 gigawatt-hours a year earlier and below estimates. The results come as the U.S. electric-vehicle market adjusts to the phase-out of federal purchase incentives and competition from Chinese automakers intensifies across markets. title: NH mountain runner representing Team USA in Skyrunning Championships - wmur.com
content: Bedford native and University of New Hampshire alum Gabby DeAngelis is training for the World Skyrunning Championships. The competition will take place in Spain's Canary Islands. One of DeAngelis' events will be an 18-mile race with a vertical climb of 6,200 feet up volcanic terrain. DeAngelis said she is honored to represent New Hampshire. She will be one of three representing Team USA. "Being part of Team USA and showing that little NH next to my name, I'm getting chills talking about it," DeAngelis said. She ran track and cross country for the UNH Wildcats. DeAngelis wants to finish the race, but the chance to represent the Granite State high above the clouds is the ultimate summit. "I love New Hampshire so much. It's such an honor. In the trail space especially, the West gets a lot of credit for producing the super awesome strong athletes... but we have some pretty good killers in New England, too," said DeAngelis. content: Harvard, welcome to the 2026-2027 college football season! What better way to welcome one of the oldest teams in college football history to the new season than a must-see Ivy-CAA matchup live on FloCollege. The Crimson will take on New Hampshire to open the Crimson's season in a game that's massively important for both teams. Here's what you need to know about Harvard vs. New Hampshire on Saturday, Sept. 19. The biggest news in the offseason for Harvard was the loss of their senior quarterback Jaden Craig, who transferred to TCU for his last season of college football. In 2024 and 2025, Craig combined for 5,299 yards, 48 touchdowns to just 9 interceptions. He was First Team All-Ivy League in 2025 and was one of the most sought after transfer quarterbacks in the nation. Dante Torres will take over starting duties in 2026 for the Crimson. He appeared in five games for Harvard in 2025, going 8-13, 153 yards, 1 touchdown and 1 interception. Torres has big shoes to fill, and it’s unlikely he’s going to produce at the same level as Craig. But he’ll have an opportunity to start off the season on a positive note against a New Hampshire defense that allowed 28 points against Albany and 66 points vs Syracuse. Harvard running back Xaviah Bascon is arguably the top skill position player in the Ivy League. Coming off a Second Team All-Ivy League selection in 2025, Bascon is primed to take a step forward as the focal point of the Crimson offense. Running back Joquez Smith for the Wildcats is coming off a season-best performance against Stonehill where he ran for 122 yards and 3 touchdowns. He splits carries with Myles Thomason, who has run for just under 1400 yards during his time with UNH. Saturday’s dogfight could come down to who can stop the run. Keeping Bascon under check and forcing Torres to throw could lead to a long game for Harvard. On the other hand, UNH is 0-2 when rushing for under 65 yards this season, with their one win coming on a 153 rushing yard performance. Whoever controls the line of scrimmage will control the game. UNH coach Sean Goldrich is one of the youngest head coaches in college football at just 33 years old. He comes from an offensive background, being a quarterback coach at Yale and Delaware. Harvard is led by Andrew Audrich, the 43-year-old who spent years as an offensive coach at Rutgers and Princeton, has led the Crimson to a 17-4 record over two seasons. The growing trend in college football is pivoting towards hiring young, offensive-minded coaches, and that’s exactly what these two teams have. These are two names to watch in head coaching searches in the future. But first, they’ll try to earn marquee wins for their programs as they climb the FCS ranks. Harvard’s 8-0 record against New Hampshire is the second most wins without a loss against any program in the school’s history (Maine, 11-0). For UNH, their 0-8 record against Harvard is the most amount of losses they have against ANY program without a win. The two schools went 85 years without playing each other before renewing the matchup in 2024, with Harvard winning 28-23. title: Seabirds on the Wing - University of New Hampshire
content: The Gulf of Maine is a literal marine hotspot, warming three times faster than ocean waters elsewhere over the past four decades. These changes affect marine life, including the distribution and abundance of fishes that other species, such as seabirds, depend on for food. UNH researchers studied how shifts in the populations of forage fish — fish species that are important sources of food — affect the ability of one seabird, the common tern, to forage efficiently in order to produce eggs and provide food for their chicks after hatching. While common terns are highly mobile and able to cover large distances, the study’s findings indicate that increased movement effort when prey is locally scarce does not improve chick diet or survival, highlighting the far-reaching effects of the changing marine environment. Having to fly farther to catch fish may negatively affect egg laying and tern chick survival. In a paper published in Movement Ecology, a research team led by UNH scientists Aliya Caldwell, Elizabeth Craig, and Nathan Furey, presents data on tern movement, reproductive productivity, and chick provisioning collected across four breeding seasons. Furey, associate professor of biological sciences in the College of Life Sciences and Agriculture, Caldwell, a biological sciences doctoral candidate in Furey’s lab, and Craig, director of seabird research at the Shoals Marine Lab and affiliate faculty of the department of biological sciences, worked on White and Seavey Islands at the south end of the Isles of Shoals. The islands are home to the site of the largest common tern breeding colony in the Gulf of Maine and are managed annually by Shoals Marine Laboratory researchers in collaboration with the New Hampshire Fish and Game Department. “Our results suggest that even though adult common terns can adjust their movements when forage fish locations shift, longer distance movements to find food may not improve chick survival rates,” says Caldwell. “The findings underscore the importance of implementing proactive management for foraging seabirds, as warming waters may increasingly lead to years of high foraging effort, poor diet, and low reproductive success.” The Gulf of Maine has historically been a rich hunting ground for common terns, boasting large populations of forage fishes such as herrings, hakes, and sand lances. These fishes are the right size and shape for terns to capture and ingest, with herrings and sand lances providing particularly high energy density. While there have always been annual variations in the exact amounts of fish available to the terns and the areas in which they congregate, the recent warming trends have led to significant shifts in abundance and location. Also, warmer water species such as Atlantic butterfish, a wide-bodied fish that most tern chicks are unable to swallow, are now moving into the Gulf. The Isles of Shoals are located about six miles off the New Hampshire coast. The researchers deployed solar-powered GPS tags on adult common terns to monitor their movements during the 2021–2024 breeding seasons. They also collected prey provisioning  — the actual prey fed to the chicks — and reproductive productivity data including egg laying and chick survival from nests within the colony. Their observations indicated that two of the years, 2022 and 2024, had ample forage fish availability near the White and Seavey Islands colony, while local prey availability was lower in 2021 and 2023, causing foraging movement effort to increase. During 2021 and 2023, the foraging trips extended to include the waters off central and southern Massachusetts, nearly 100 miles from the colony. Early-season access to prey is essential for egg laying, and common terns rely on energy from real-time food acquisition to produce eggs. The data showed that the years with plentiful nearby forage fish saw more eggs laid and much better chick survival than in the years that adults had to seek fish farther away. “Looking ahead, we recently received [National Science Foundation] funding to investigate the role of individual variations in foraging behavior — that is, do some birds move or feed differently than others?” says Furey. “Perhaps some birds can be flexible and change their diets or movements within a breeding season, with an impact on chick survival. In addition to common terns, Aliya will expand her work to include roseate terns, Arctic terns, great black-backed gulls, black guillemots, and Atlantic puffins at colonies throughout the Gulf of Maine.” The importance of the research is underscored by current projections that environmental changes will further accelerate shifts in forage fish communities. If the projections are accurate, increased foraging effort during breeding seasons may lead to increased movement effort and decreased reproductive success, threatening seabird populations in the Gulf of Maine and elsewhere. title: Justice Foreclosed? - University of New Hampshire
content: Every year, schools and government agencies join the nation in observing Constitution Day and Citizenship Day the week before and after Sept. 17, the anniversary of the signing of the Constitution. Federal courts participate by offering educational resources and experiences in their communities. Below, UNH associate professor of political science Susan Siggelakis pens a piece entitled "Justice Foreclosed?" This essay considers the Supreme Court case Pung v. Isabella County, Michigan. Here is the opinion. If you’ve lived in New Hampshire for any length of time, you may have heard people complaining about their property tax bill. Twice a year, homeowners receive the dreaded missive in the mail, perhaps procrastinating for a few weeks or months before reluctantly forking over thousands of dollars to their city or town government. Even if you live in an apartment, you will see this tax reflected in your ever-increasing rent bill as your landlord, too, pays this hefty exaction. Though it may seem that residents are paying simply for the privilege of living in their own places, the fact is that the proceeds from these local taxes pay for local schools, fire departments, libraries, road maintenance and other key municipal departments and services. Moving to another state is no solution. Throughout the United States, property taxes are a ubiquitous feature of modern life. Of course, in many cases property taxes may be discounted for senior citizens, veterans, or owners who chose to put some of their property in a conservation easement, for example. Yet, for almost all of us, it is our duty as good citizens to pay up, a civic act one that helps maintain and improve our quality of life. What happens if we don’t pay our property tax? One Michigan couple found out the hard way, with their dispute going all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court. Their dispute began in 2020. The Pungs, who had inherited their home from a deceased relation, lived full time in their dwelling and considered it their permanent home. In Michigan and numerous other states, (but not New Hampshire!), a vacation home or second property is taxed at a higher rate than a primary residence. For some disputed and unclear reasons their Isabella, Michigan county government taxed the Pungs’ home as if was a secondary property. The bill was $2,241.93. Though they attempted to clear this up, in the end the Pungs failed to persuade the tax officials that this was their primary residence. They also rejected several options offered by the county to end the stalemate. They refused to pay it. In the end, as is common throughout the states when people default on property taxes, the county foreclosed legally on the home. County officials later auctioned it off to the highest bidder for about $76,000, even though the home itself had been recently assessed as being worth $194,000. From the $76,000, the government took out the default amount, and returned the surplus, $73,766, to the Pungs. In doing so the county again complied with historical practice and state and local laws. The Pungs, having now lost their home, claimed that they should have received the surplus money from the $194,000 which was the assessed value of their home. This would have been about $192,000, much more than they received after the auction. Do the federal courts, applying the U.S. Constitution, have anything to say about this? Indeed they do. The Pungs were able to file their suit in federal district court, because they rested their argument on what is called a “federal question,” (i.e. a dispute about the meaning of a federal statute, a federal regulation or treaty, or the U.S. Constitution). First, they claimed that the Fourteenth Amendment’s due process clause had been violated because of the many procedural irregularities in the foreclosure procedures. For example, the Pungs claimed they did not receive the notice of foreclosure until after the county’s deadline, and that the $2,241.93 amount was not in the original tax bill that they had received. The 14th Amendment reads, “No state shall deprive any person of life, liberty or property without due process of law.” Except for being directed at the states instead of the national government, this replicates the Fifth Amendment’s provision. More important for this discussion is that the Pungs claimed the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment of the United States Constitution had been violated when they did not receive the surplus from a “fair market value” of the sale of their foreclosed home. That amendment reads in relevant part “[nor shall any person] be deprived of life, liberty or property without due process of law; nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation.” The single district court judge, relying on various precedents, ruled against the Pungs, as did the three-judge panel of the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals. The Pungs then appealed to the United States Supreme Court, which granted the writ of certiorari to hear the case. Like the U.S. Court of Appeals, the U.S. Supreme Court is an appellate court, whose function is to ensure that courts below did not make any errors in interpreting and applying federal law. The Pungs had argued that centuries of “eminent domain” decisions, that is, instances when a state or city takes someone’s property for public use and just compensation is given, should guide the Court’s opinion. In centuries of legal opinions, the constitutional phrase “just compensation” has generally meant fair market value. An example of eminent domain would be when the state of New Jersey in the late 1960s took hundreds of houses adjacent to a stretch of the New Jersey Turnpike to widen the turnpike to accommodate increasing traffic in the late 1960s. It paid homeowners compensation based on the current, assessed value of their houses. Many homeowners were pleased with the ‘fair market value’ amount they received, as it allowed them to move to nicer homes elsewhere. If numerous judges upholding eminent domain takings have equated ‘just compensation’ with the fair market value of the property, then the same rule should apply here, they asserted. Unfortunately for the Pungs, the Court’s decision was unanimous, 9-0. It upheld the rulings of the two courts below on the constitutional issue surrounding the amount of the surplus. All ruled that the county had complied with the Takings Clause in returning the surplus from the foreclosed sale. The county was not constitutionally required to return a higher surplus from the assessed value of the house prior to its sale. The Court rejected the Pungs’ argument for three reasons: 1) their use of irrelevant eminent domain precedents (prior decisions involving the Takings Clause); 2) the problems the Pungs’ new constitutional rule would pose for municipal governance as well as other taxpayers; 3) the noncontroversial practice of foreclosure sales over the course of United States history. The Court made quick work of dismissing the eminent domain precedents, arguing that the Pungs were comparing apples to oranges. As Associate Justice Alito, writing for the Court commented, “what might be just in one context may not be just in another.’” Even in eminent domain cases, he noted, courts sometimes deviated from the fair market value rule and found different types of compensation to be “just,” for instance “when market value has been too difficult to find, or when its application would result in manifest injustice to owner or the public.” In addition, in eminent domain takings, homeowners have generally done nothing wrong, unlike delinquent taxpayers. The second main prong of the Court’s opinion was the practical concerns of local and state government: “Tax sales are meant to collect unpaid taxes without undue delay and administrative expense.” Were towns and cities required to sell foreclosed properties the way homeowners typically do, they would either have to sell the property themselves or hire a real-estate agent. In the interim before a full value sale, which would be uncertain and likely take many months, the municipality would be deprived of the unpaid taxes. If the town or city couldn’t or wouldn’t sell the foreclosed property, the new legal rule advocated by the Pungs would mean that the municipality would still have to pay the former owners the full market value, a cost which would ultimately be shouldered by local taxpayers. This would most likely be done by increasing residents’ property tax bills! Alito writes “so for taxpayers as a group, the demise of tax sales might be a most unwelcome development.” The third prong of the opinion rests on the Court’s opinion of both what happened in the past with tax sales, but also what didn’t happen: “Tax sales have been an accepted means for governments to collect debts since the earliest days of our nation. If the takings clauses had rendered these sales untenable, they would have presumably faded away….”. Although Associate Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch both agreed with the main ruling, they noted some irregularities. In a concurring opinion, Justice Thomas (joined by Gorsuch in part) asserted that the Court’s opinion neglected the many traditional practices and legal norms that had historically protected debtors’ property from egregious takings, as he characterized the one here. First, he noted that it was well-established that the government had to try and sell the taxpayer’s personal property before it could try and take land or buildings. This was especially important when a small debt might conceivably put a family out of their home. If these ‘chattels’ were sufficient to discharge the tax debt, then land and homes were off limits to the government. In fact, if the government took more than what was required to discharge the debt, the property owner could sue the government for trespass or trover (a common law action to recover property or receive equal compensation of said property). In the past, judges had generally scrutinized foreclosure proceedings carefully to make sure that parties were notified in timely, complete fashion. Thomas also asserts that, in many cases, judges tried to ensure that auction prices were as close to market value as possible. Anchoring the right to property in Anglo-American political and legal thought, he cites the famous British jurist William Blackstone statement that “the law of the land… postpones even public necessity to the sacred and inviolable rights of property.” Thomas concludes: “the government exists to protect property; property does not exist to support the government.” In the end, the Court only settled the constitutional question, which now becomes precedent, a guide for all judges around the country should they encounter a similar legal dispute between government and a property owner. It sent back down (remanded) the case back to the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals to deal with the Pungs’ particular claims of the allegedly unfair procedures employed by Isabella County. It is certainly possible that the county will be held to have violated the “due process” that it was required to afford the Pungs under the Fourteenth Amendment. But that’s a story for another Constitution Day! Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: This Dividend Stock Is Staging a Turnaround in 2026 and Pays More Than 2.4% - inkl

For much of 2025, UnitedHealth Group (UNH) looked like a company under siege as higher medical costs and weaker margins rattled investors. UNH stock sold off sharply, and questions emerged around the company’s earnings outlook as well as the health of its long-standing growth story. That picture is starting to improve in 2026. UnitedHealth's latest results showed a clear turnaround in profitability as it generated $112 billion in revenue and $8 billion in earnings from operations. Management also raised the company's full-year adjusted EPS outlook to a range of $19.50 to $20 and increased its operating cash flow forecast to about $24 billion. Those moves suggest UnitedHealth sees its recovery as more than a short-term earnings rebound. This improving earnings and cash flow profile carries particular weight for dividend investors, as UnitedHealth now pays an annualized dividend of $9.28 per share, offering a yield above 2.4%. With shares rebounding from their 2025 lows, can UnitedHealth’s improving margins and cash generation support both continued dividend growth and further upside? Let’s take a closer look. Based in Eden Prairie, Minnesota, UnitedHealth Group operates UnitedHealthcare, its health-benefits arm, and Optum, which provides pharmacy benefits, care delivery, data, and technology services. With a market capitalization of $337 billion, the company serves consumers, employers, governments, care providers, and health plans across its insurance and services platforms. On Sept. 15, UNH stock closed the session at $375.93 per share. The stock has gained 15% year-to-date (YTD) and more than 11% over the past 52 weeks. UNH stock has a PEG ratio of 1.4 times, which is below the sector median of about 1.8 times. Meanwhile, the price-to-cash flow (P/CF) multiple of about 18 times is above the sector median of around 15 times. UnitedHealth currently pays a forward annual dividend of $9.28 per share, which equates to a 2.4% yield. Investors who owned UNH stock as of the Sept. 14 record date will receive a $2.32 quarterly payment on Sept. 22. That payout is backed by improving earnings momentum. On July 16, the company reported second-quarter 2026 results that included $112 billion in revenue. The figure came in slightly ahead of the $110.6 billion consensus estimate and was flat with the prior year. Meanwhile, adjusted EPS of $6.38 beat the $4.88 consensus estimate. UnitedHealth's medical care ratio was 86.7% for Q2, helped by product changes, improved medical management, and better-aligned pricing. This measure included $860 million of favorable prior-period development, mainly tied to 2026 service dates. UnitedHealthcare served 48.5 million consumers, generating $86 billion in revenue and $3.9 billion in earnings. Optum supported more than 120 million consumers, generated $65.7 billion in revenue, and delivered $4 billion in earnings in Q2. Operating margin expanded to 7.1% from 4.6% a year earlier, reflecting a meaningful improvement in profitability. That progress supported $8 billion of earnings from operations and a 4.9% net margin. Cash flow from operations was $11.1 billion, equal to 1.9 times net income, providing substantial coverage for the dividend. The debt-to-capital ratio was 41.2% as of June 30, 2026. Margin expanded 160 basis points year-over-year (YOY), adding support to UNH’s broader turnaround thesis. UnitedHealth Group is pairing its operational recovery with a larger commitment to shareholders. Management now expects to repurchase at least $5 billion of common stock in 2026, raising its original buyback target. The firm had already repurchased $4 billion of shares through mid-July. The company is also directing resources toward programs that could improve affordability, access, and member engagement over time. UnitedHealth’s partnership with University of Tennessee Health Sciences will expand health hubs into more Tennessee communities. The initiative connects residents with local support and resources that address health-related social needs. In July, UnitedHealthcare also introduced a new spending account benefit that gives eligible consumers greater flexibility in using health plan funds. The offering expands choices for qualified healthcare and everyday wellness expenses. In addition, UnitedHealthcare expanded child and family behavioral coaching access to 13 million commercial members. The program provides families with support for behavioral and emotional challenges beyond conventional insurance coverage. Together, these initiatives show how UnitedHealth is approaching its recovery on two fronts. The buybacks return excess capital to shareholders, while care access and engagement programs could help the company manage costs and strengthen member relationships over time. UnitedHealth Group is due to report its Q3 2026 results on Oct. 27. Analysts expect EPS of $4.03, up 38% YOY from earnings of $2.92 per share. On July 22, Bernstein kept a “Buy” rating on UNH stock and assigned a $512 price target, pointing to 35% potential upside from current levels. Around the same time, UBS reiterated its “Buy” rating and lifted its target to $490 from $460, citing a stronger-than-expected Q2 performance and improving Medicare Advantage trends. The broader Wall Street view remains constructive. UNH stock has a consensus “Strong Buy” rating among 26 analysts with coverage. The average price target of $480.81 points to potential upside of 27% from current levels. UnitedHealth’s 2026 turnaround looks increasingly credible. Improving margins, stronger cash flow, a larger buyback plan, and a $9.28 annual dividend provide tangible support for the UNH stock investment case. Wall Street also sees meaningful upside if Medicare Advantage trends and Optum’s recovery continue. Overall, the most likely path forward is further progress, although quarterly results may remain uneven. Support for socialism stronger among younger voters A July 29 University of New Hampshire poll showing that half of Vermonters view socialism positively — compared with 42% who view capitalism positively — suggests the word “socialism” has considerable appeal in Vermont. But a closer look at the poll shows that support for socialism, membership in the Democratic Socialists of America and the electoral value of a DSA endorsement are three different things. The July Green Mountain State Poll found 51% of Vermont residents had a very or somewhat positive view of socialism, while 31% viewed it negatively. Capitalism was evenly divided: 42% positive and 42% negative. Another 14% were neutral or had no opinion about socialism, compared with 12% for capitalism. That does not mean half of Vermonters identify themselves as socialists or support the Democratic Socialists of America. The poll asked separately about attitudes toward an ideology and attitudes toward a political organization. The distinction is especially clear in the DSA numbers. Just 2% of Vermonters said they currently belong to DSA and another 1% said they were former members. Half said they had heard of the organization and understood what it was, but 19% had heard of it without knowing much about it, 22% had never heard of it and 7% were unsure. In other words, about half of those surveyed did not claim a solid understanding of DSA, despite the relatively favorable statewide numbers for socialism itself. Among the 878 respondents who had heard of DSA, 47% viewed the organization positively, 31% negatively, 15% were neutral and 7% were unsure. The partisan divide was large: the poll reported that 71% of Democrats had positive feelings about DSA, while 89% of Republicans had negative feelings. Independents were almost evenly split, with 39% positive and 35% negative. The poll also tested whether a DSA endorsement would actually influence a vote. Among respondents familiar with DSA, 37% said an endorsement would make them more likely to support a candidate, while 30% said it would make them less likely. Another 26% said it would have little or no effect and 7% were unsure. Among self-described socialists, 86% said a DSA endorsement would make them more likely to vote for a candidate. That fell to 62% among progressives, 45% among liberals and just 9% among moderates. In a column set to be published this weekend, former Rep. Bob Stannard of Manchester (himself leaning left but not a socialist, despite incorrect description on yesterday’s edition – Editor) defined Capitalism and Socialism. Capitalism: “Capitalism is an economic system where private individuals and businesses own the tools, factories, and resources used to make goods, rather than the government. According to the International Monetary Fund, capitalism relies on private ownership, profit, and competition.” Socialism: “Socialism is an economic and political system where the community or the government owns and controls the major means of production—such as factories, tools, and large businesses—instead of private individuals. According to the general Socialism Definition & Meaning from Merriam-Webster, the core idea is that shared ownership helps distribute wealth more evenly and provides basic needs like healthcare and education to everyone.” Age may help explain why socialism performs comparatively well in Vermont. The poll found 60% of Vermonters ages 18 to 34 had a positive view of socialism, compared with 25% who viewed capitalism positively. Among those 35 to 49, socialism was viewed positively by 54%, compared with 31% for capitalism. The relationship reversed among older Vermonters. Among those ages 50 to 64, 49% viewed capitalism positively and 47% viewed socialism positively. Among residents 65 and older, capitalism led 56% to 44%. About half of Vermonters under 50 viewed capitalism negatively, according to UNH. The poll also provides an important limit on what “positive toward socialism” means. Socialism did not translate into comparable acceptance of communism. Only 11% of Vermonters viewed communism positively, while 73% viewed it negatively. Fascism was viewed negatively by 90%. The ideological cross-tabs sharpen the distinction further. Nearly all respondents who identified as socialists viewed socialism positively, as did 78% of progressives and 60% of liberals. Moderates were nearly evenly divided, while 91% of conservatives and 69% of libertarians viewed socialism negatively. Vermont also stood apart from its northern New England neighbors. UNH found 50% positive toward socialism in Vermont, compared with 35% in New Hampshire and 39% in Maine. DSA was viewed positively by 47% of Vermonters familiar with it, versus 30% in both New Hampshire and Maine. Taken together, the poll indicates that “socialism” has become a relatively positive political label for many Vermonters, particularly younger residents and people on the political left. It does not establish that a majority of Vermonters identify as socialists, belong to DSA, support a particular socialist economic program, or would vote for a DSA-backed candidate. The Green Mountain State Poll was conducted online July 15-20 by the UNH Survey Center. It included 1,119 Vermont residents and reported a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. Results were weighted for sex, age, education, region and Vermont’s 2024 election results. UNH also cautioned that question wording, question order, nonresponse and other non-sampling errors can affect survey results. Subscribe to get the latest posts sent to your email. The next quarterly UnitedHealth (NYSE: UNH) dividend is coming next week, on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, when all shareholders of record as of the close of business on September 14, 2026, will receive $2.32 per share. With the payment unchanged from the previous quarter paid on June 23, investors holding 100 UNH shares will once again receive $232 in quarterly cash dividends. Those holding 50 shares will receive $116, while those holding 10 shares will receive $23. Combined with the first quarter payment, which was slightly lower at $2.2, the total payout over the past three quarters will amount to $685 on September 22. If the fourth quarter payout remains unchanged, investors will have made $917 per 100 shares in passive income in 2026 overall – roughly $2.5 per day. title: Race to Replace Democrat Senator in New Hampshire Shifts Toward GOP - Newsweek
content: SCOTUS Blocks Mail-Ballot Restrictions, McConnell Senate Return, Trump Dismisses AI Concerns: The Bulletin, Sept. 15 SCOTUS Blocks Mail-Ballot Restrictions, McConnell Senate Return, Trump Dismisses AI Concerns: The Bulletin, Sept. 15 EU Ambassador Addresses Canada Becoming An Associate Member SCOTUS Blocks Mail-Ballot Restrictions, McConnell Senate Return, Trump Dismisses AI Concerns: The Bulletin, Sept. 15 The race to replace retiring Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen in New Hampshire has shifted toward Republicans, with The Cook Political Report moving the contest from Lean Democratic to Toss Up as former Republican Senator John Sununu and Democratic Representative Chris Pappas prepare for November's general election. The shift comes after newer polls show a seemingly competitive race between Sununu and Pappas. A University of New Hampshire (UNH) poll conducted in late August found Sununu at 45 percent and Pappas at 43 percent among likely voters. A Saint Anselm College poll conducted earlier that month showed Pappas leading Sununu 48 percent to 41 percent. The race has also attracted significant spending from national Republicans, who are on pace to hold a $20 million advantage in New Hampshire, Cook notes. "Sununu allies have already outspent pro-Pappas groups by almost a 2-1 margin," according to the forecaster. Meanwhile, midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during midterm elections. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority in the House and Senate. Former Vice President Kamala Harris narrowly won the state in the 2024 presidential election over President Donald Trump by under 3 percent. Newsweek reached out to Sununu and Pappas' campaigns via email on Tuesday for comment. Recent polling on the race has somewhat narrowed compared to earlier surveys. UNH had Pappas ahead of Sununu 49 percent to 42 percent in April and 47 percent to 44 percent in June. RealClearPolitics currently lists the contest as a Toss Up as well, with its polling average showing Pappas at 45.5 percent and Sununu at 41.5 percent. A September co/efficient survey shows the candidates now tied at 46 percent each. The poll adds that 9 percent are undecided. Pappas' favorability in the poll is 37 percent compared to an unfavorable rating of 51 percent and 13 percent have no opinion. Sununu's favorability rating in the poll is 41 percent compared to a 47 percent unfavorable rating, while 12 percent had no opinion. The poll surveyed 958 likely general election voters in the state from September 9-11, 2026, and has a margin of error of 3.15 percent. In the write-up on the race, Cook said in part, "When it comes to the Senate race, some Democratic polling has the race within the margin of error (though others have Pappas with a more comfortable lead) but GOP polling has shown the race tied or with Sununu ahead. It is possible that most of the undecided voters will ultimately break for Democrats, but it’s hard to forecast outcomes in the famously independently-minded state until the race fully engages." Craig Agranoff, Florida Atlantic University political professor, told Newsweek on Tuesday when asked if this is concerning for Democrats, "It’s a red flag because of the combination, not just one poll. You have a well-known Republican in John Sununu, an open Democratic seat, tightening surveys, and outside Republican money flowing in. That is how a Lean Democrat race becomes a toss up. It does not mean Democrats lose NH. It means they have to spend time and money here instead of putting all of it into flipping Republican seats." The latest shift is particularly significant because the Granite State has not elected a Republican senator since 2010. Sununu, who previously represented New Hampshire in the Senate, won the Republican nomination earlier this month, while Pappas won the Democratic nomination. Both candidates now face a general election campaign that is expected to receive significant national attention as Democrats seek to regain control of the Senate as Republicans hope to hold on. Defending ECAC tournament champion Dartmouth College was predicted to finish second in the conference standings in the league's  men's hockey preseason coaches' poll that was released on Wednesday. Dartmouth received two first-place votes and tallied 110 points, second to Quinnipiac University (10 first-place votes, 120 points). The Big Green won a program-record 23 games and made their first NCAA Division I tournament appearance since 1980 last year. Junior forward Hayden Stavroff, the ECAC Player of the Year last year, headlines Dartmouth's key returners. Stavroff, fellow junior forward Hank Cleaves and senior goaltender Emmett Croteau were named to the All-ECAC preseason team. Bedford native Rand Pecknold is entering his 33rd season coaching Quinnipiac, which has won the last six ECAC regular season titles. In the Hockey East preseason coaches poll, the University of New Hampshire placed ninth in the 11-team league. The Wildcats earned 35 points in the poll, finishing ahead of UMass Lowell (31 points) and Vermont (22 points). The Wildcats went 14-20-1 overall and 8-15-1 in Hockey East play last season. Providence College (106 points) topped the poll, receiving eight first-place votes. Massachusetts (98 points, one first-place vote), Boston University (87 points, two first-place votes), Boston College (86 points) and Connecticut (73 points) rounded out the top five. Defending Hockey East champion Merrimack College placed sixth in the poll with 68 points. UNH will open its 2026-27 campaign at Quinnipiac on Friday, Oct. 2. The Wildcats will also play at Dartmouth on Sunday, Dec. 13. The Big Green open their season by hosting Alaska Fairbanks at Thompson Arena on Halloween night (7).
